sections.context: SPEC section 9 and D14, D15, D19. Every later feature writes events (sling sent, reply landed, agent done) and blobs (packets, UI code). The record must exist first, and its formats are API (B5).
sections.approach: The core defines events and blob ids as pure, versioned data. slingerd owns one SQLite file per machine (rusqlite, bundled) and is its only reader and writer. The CLI gets record and blob verbs. Views and the thinking record (O3) are not built until the log has real events.

sections.context: SPEC D5, D6, D7, K1, K3, K5, O5. The canvas is a native rebuild and the largest piece of work. The model and the file format must exist before the packet, the agent commands or the app's canvas pane can be built.
sections.approach: The canvas is one deep module in the core: items, operations, undo, geometry queries and the file codec. Its file format is designed twice and then picked (B6). slingerd is the only writer of a canvas file (K5) and serves canvases over verbs with a change feed. The tldraw importer reads the real board `idea.tldraw` as its fixture (B8).

sections.context: SPEC section 6, D8, D9 and the Spike B result. An agent gets a packet, not a screenshot. Spike B showed 44% of the screenshot cost and three defects to fix: long strokes join clusters, distance alone is not enough to cluster, and a crop over the image size limit needs tiles.
sections.approach: The packet is one deep module in the core. The format is designed twice and then picked (B6). Clustering, rendering, the index and the delta are separate seeds behind one interface: canvas and marker in, packet out. Rendering is pure Rust so the core stays free of FFI. The real board is the fixture.

The three Spike B findings each have a test.

sections.context: SPEC sections 5 and 10, D10, D16, D20, O6 and Spike C. A sling goes to a session that already exists and remembers earlier slings. The server must know its workspaces, hold the Claude Code sessions, and know each agent's status.
sections.approach: The core owns the workspace definition and its rules. slingerd keeps the workspace and session lists and, as decided by the owner, holds one Claude Code process open per session (stream input, stream output), as Spike C proved. There is no harness trait (B7): Claude Code reaches Slinger through the CLI and its hooks. Slinger builds no durable-agent machinery (D20).

A session cannot read outside the limits set for it.

sections.context: SPEC sections 6 and 7 and Spike C. The sling is the core move: select, prompt, packet, agent, reply, record. The agent answers with things on the canvas through a small command set that is built to grow.
sections.approach: Each agent command is one CLI verb that follows the CLI contract. `sling send` joins the pieces that already exist: the packet, the session and the record. A new ability is always a new verb; existing verbs do not change meaning.

sections.context: SPEC sections 5, 11, P4, P5, P6, D2, D12, D17, D18, O4. The client is the window: panes, canvas and input. It holds no durable state. Every action is a key command in a plain-text config file.
sections.approach: Keep the app's layering from ARCHITECTURE.md: pure `scene` and `layout` modules decide, `platform` draws, `backend` talks to the daemon. Config and key dispatch are pure modules with tests. The pane layout is stored by the server in the workspace. Dictation is Flick's; Slinger has no speech code.

sections.context: SPEC D5, D6, K1, K2, O2 and Spike A. The canvas pane is where the user thinks with a pen. Spike A passed with plain AppKit: one view, smoothed paths at a constant width, mouse coalescing off, repaint of the changed box only.
sections.approach: D6 is the limit: pen at a constant width, eraser, lasso, text, box, arrow, pages, undo, endless pan and zoom. Nothing else. Viewport and scene code are pure and tested; AppKit code stays in `platform`. Ink shows at once and is sent to the server off the main thread, so a write never waits (P7). Pen feel is judged by the owner (K2).

sections.context: SPEC section 8, D13, D19, K4, O1, O8. An agent UI is a small interface that an agent builds for one task. It can be a pane or an item on a canvas. It is untrusted code: no network, no file access, only the bridge.
sections.approach: The code a live item runs is designed twice and then picked (B6); the first form in O1 is HTML in a sandboxed web view. The code lives in the record as a blob, named and versioned (D19). The bridge has two calls: read the context, reply with JSON. The first live item, the 'send to agent' button, is built in.
